THE ARITHMETIC: `highway_speed`'s camera drives WITH the traffic, so a vehicle in an adjacent lane is near-parallel to the camera heading and therefore near end-on, which is this metric's own window. Session 6b measured 9 of 18 and this session's predecessor 11 of 22 vehicles carrying a readable ROOFLINE, and the roofline excludes exactly the near-end-on half — so the complement is about half the measured population, 11 of 22, and 5 is under that with the same margin `minProfileMeasured` took. THE FLOOR IS WRITTEN BEFORE THE MEASUREMENT AND IS NOT MOVED AFTERWARDS. Note what it CANNOT distinguish on its own and why `nWidthDeclinedBias` is reported beside it: a population that emptied because the camera never looked end-on, and one that emptied because every subject's parts are too long for `maxWidthBias`. The delivered fleet is the second, which is why the count and the decline count are both printed.

pedestrian.$NO_SILHOUETTE_ASSERTION: NOTHING BELOW MEASURES A PEDESTRIAN'S SILHOUETTE, AND SESSION 10 DID NOT WRITE ONE. Recorded here rather than left to be inferred from two green numbers, because a green gate and an absent gate are indistinguishable in every report this project produces (CONTRACT §7.1) and this is the SEVENTH instance of that pattern. WHAT THE TWO BELOW ACTUALLY MEASURE. `minWidthRoughness` is `profileRoughness` on the mask's row widths: it asks whether the outline DOUBLES BACK down the figure — narrow head, wide shoulders, narrower legs with a gap. A stack of axis-aligned boxes has exactly that, so it scores well: the session-9 box bodies measured 1.012 (recorded in streetlife.js at the time) and session 10's lofted bodies measure 1.3, both against a floor of 0.35. The floor separates a person from a bollard and it cannot separate a person from a stack of prisms. `minChromaClusters` counts garment chromaticities and is a statement about the palette, not about a shape; it was 10 on boxes and is 8 on lofts. THE PROPERTY NEITHER SEES is the one §7.5 named for the vehicles one axis over: within the torso, is the width a function of height, or is the figure a constant-width column between its shoulders and its hips. WHAT WAS TRIED AND WHY IT IS NOT HERE. The obvious metric is a torso-band taper, (max-min)/max of the row widths between about 0.50 and 0.83 of the subject's own height. It does not discriminate: a figure with its arms down has arms filling the gap beside the waist, so the FRONT silhouette of a real body is nearly constant width from shoulder to hip too, and the metric would reject the delivered loft as readily as the boxes. The property that does separate them is the SHAPE of the width profile rather than its range — a box stack's is piecewise constant with long plateaus at exactly one value, a loft's varies continuously — so the discriminator is a plateau fraction with a ceiling, or the same statistic inverted into a floor. THAT METRIC NEEDS ITS OWN CONTROLS AND THEY MUST GO THROUGH THE RENDER PATH (§7.3.1): a vertical prism and a vertically stepped one, swept over the distances and headings the pedestrian population actually contains, both directions required at every view. Two of this project's metrics have been written without that and both answered the same number to every shape. It is a session's work and session 10 spent its budget on the geometry and on `night_rain`; the analysis is written down here so the next session starts from it rather than from scratch. UNTIL THEN: the pedestrians' silhouette is asserted by NOTHING, the two floors below are about outline structure and palette, and no number in this file should be read as a verdict on whether a pedestrian reads as a person. The 10 m and 40 m frames in tools/shot-out are the whole of the evidence, and §10 step 4 says numbers are necessary and not sufficient - here there are none.

lightRoles.$comment: A CEILING PER ROLE ON THE CLUSTERED LIGHT POOL, READ OFF THE LIVE POOL BY `lights.countByRole`. Until this session `role` was a free-form tag with exactly one consumer and every shipping light left it null, so 'how many slots does street lighting have and how many does traffic' was a question the world could not answer about itself. It can now, and the answer is asserted rather than argued.
lightRoles.$derivation: 384 slots. Measured at boot and printed there: 52 block + 196 streetlamp = 248 static, 96 reserved for traffic = 344, margin 40. THE 40 IS THE STREET-LEVEL ALLOWANCE 4a LEFT AND IT IS WHAT SHOPS AND STALLS DRAW ON. This session spends 12 of it — see `streetLevel` in tools/city-budget.json for which fixtures earn a slot and which are emissive geometry — leaving 28. The ceilings below are per role and their sum is 384 by construction; each one is a claim that can fail on its own, which a single total cannot.
lightRoles.$requireEveryLightHasARole: Every light in the pool declares one. A null role is a slot nobody is accountable for, and the pool filling up is exactly the failure that arrives with no name attached to it. Turned on this session; `unrolled` must be 0.
lightRoles.$aircraft: SESSION 20, ITEM 5. ONE SLOT, AND IT IS A CEILING AND A FLOOR ON THE SAME NUMBER because the population is exactly one: the searchlight under the orbiting helicopter. Everything else in the air is emissive geometry at zero slots, by the same argument `trafficLights.$content` makes about tail lamps — the pool a 40 cd position light throws from 400 m is nothing, and what makes an aircraft read at night is the emitter itself. THE FLOOR IS THE HALF THAT EARNS ITS PLACE: a ceiling of 1 is satisfied by a searchlight that stopped being created, which reads as excellent pool margin, and that is precisely the failure `$minOccupancyMargin` and the `traffic` floor were both written for. What it spends: `roleCensus` reported traffic 96 + stall 12 + block 52 + lamp 196 = 356 of 384 before this session, so 357 of 384 after, and 27 spare.
lightRoles.$floors: A role that stopped being created reads as excellent margin. Floors are what makes the margin mean something, and they are set from the delivered counts.

winding.$comment: THE WINDING GATE, SESSION 14. `tools/windcheck.mjs` and `tools/lib/winding.mjs`. Three winding defects in three places across two sessions — the pedestrian loft (s12), the ground quad (s13) and the reveal's double rotation (s13) — every one of them geometry submitted every frame and never seen, and every one of them invisible to six gates for the same reason: THE SILHOUETTE OF A CONVEX SOLID IS IDENTICAL WHICHEVER SHELL IS DRAWN. Nothing in this project has ever asked which shell reached the frame.
winding.$pixelFree: NOT ONE OF THE THREE TESTS READS A PIXEL, and session 22 turned that from a property into the reason a software rasteriser no longer refuses this gate. `volume` is a signed sum over the triangle order; `normals` compares the authored attribute with the geometric normal, weighted by area; `facing` computes front-facing AREA toward an eye point in world space through `matrixWorld` and three's own `frontFaceCW` rule. All three run in `harness.windingCensus()` on the CPU over geometry attributes and delivered instance matrices, and `$minNormalAgreement` below already says of itself that the whole computation is deterministic Float32 arithmetic in JS with no driver in it. WHAT WOULD INVALIDATE THIS, written down so a later session can check it rather than trust it: any threshold here that comes to read `page.screenshot()`, a `readRenderTargetPixels`, or a harness call that renders in order to answer. Add one and the refusal has to come back, beside it, the way `citycheck`'s sits beside its saturation sample. The one way a slow renderer degrades this census is an unfinished stream, and `minMeshes` and `requiredMeshes` fail on that -- a false RED, not a false green.
winding.$threeTests: volume, normals, facing — chosen because their blind spots do not overlap. volume reads the triangle order alone and needs a closed mesh, so it is blind to every open surface, which is where two of the three defects lived. normals reads the authored normal against the geometric one — CONTRACT §9.1's 'two statements about the same thing' put side by side — and is a TAUTOLOGY wherever computeVertexNormals() derived the normals from the winding, which the census detects and the row declares. facing reads the fraction of area presenting its front to an eye through the delivered instance matrices, needs no attribute, and is the only one of the three that would have caught all three defects on its own.
winding.$maxTris: 6000 triangles sampled per geometry, then strided. The census is exhaustive under that and estimates above it, and both `tris` and `sampled` are returned so a reader can see which rows are estimates. A stride cannot change the SIGN of an area majority, which is the only thing read off it — and the closedness pass, which a stride WOULD break, runs exhaustively or declines (see `closed: null`).
winding.$eyes: CONTRACT §8 lets a gate drive `poseRoute` because the placement comes from a path the gate already runs, and forbids `setShotAt` because a gate whose camera the operator chooses measures the operator. Six poses over the three gate routes at both ends and the middle: different times of day, different wetness and — the part that matters here — different chunks resident, so between them they bring the generator's whole vocabulary into the scene rather than one street's worth of it.

thresholds.$minNormalAgreement: 1.0, AND IT IS THE DELIVERED VALUE RATHER THAN A MARGIN UNDER IT. Measured over the 622 meshes whose normals were authored rather than computed, the minimum area-weighted agreement is EXACTLY 1.0000 — not one square metre of the city carries a normal pointing against its own triangle, once session 14's loft fix landed. The two negative controls read 0.0000. So the whole interval (0,1] separates them and the choice is about the SMALLEST DEFECT THAT MUST STILL FAIL: `city:ground` is one merged mesh of 210 to 243 quads, so a single mis-wound quad in it is 0.4% of its area, and any floor below 0.996 would pass it. There is no room under the delivered value that is not a licence, so the floor is the delivered value. The per-triangle classification already has a dead band — |dot| <= 0.2 counts as ambiguous and is excluded from the ratio — so a near-perpendicular smoothed normal cannot trip it, and the whole computation is deterministic Float32 arithmetic in JS with no driver in it.
thresholds.$minFrontFacing: 0.02, AND IT IS A TOLERANCE FOR THE CENSUS'S OWN STRIDE RATHER THAN A MARGIN AGAINST THE CONTENT. The defect value is EXACTLY ZERO and not approximately: a planar surface wound away from every eye presents no front-facing area at all, which is what both the session-13 ground quad and the session-14 wall-sign back faces measure. The delivered minimum over the 623 cull-eligible meshes is 0.3284 — the market stall geometry, seen from one pose — so 0.02 sits 16x under the delivered minimum and above the defect's zero. It is not zero itself because the facing pass strides instances on a large mesh, and one unrepresentative instance out of eight must not be able to lift a genuinely invisible mesh off the floor.
thresholds.$minEyes: A facing verdict taken from one viewpoint certifies one viewpoint (CONTRACT §7.3.1). Three is the minimum at which 'no eye could see it' is a statement about the geometry rather than about where the camera happened to stand. 122 of the 623 cull-eligible meshes are resident at only one pose and 33 at two; all 155 are decided by one of the other two tests, which is what `maxUnmeasured` is for.
thresholds.$maxClosedFacing: REPORTED, NOT ASSERTED. A closed shell presents about half its area to any eye; a row well above that is either not closed or is being measured through a stride that caught one face. It prints and does not fail, because the honest bound on a non-convex closed mesh is not 0.5 and nobody has derived what it is.
thresholds.$minMeshes: 400. Delivered: 627 named meshes over the six poses. A run in which the STREAMED city never arrived would still report the origin block (67), the landmarks (11), traffic (3), the pedestrian builds and the stalls that ride with them, the rain and the sky (4) — about 95 in total. 400 sits between that failure and the delivered figure, so it catches the one thing this floor is for: a census taken of a world that had not turned up. It is a COUNT, so it does not drift (CONTRACT §9 rule 6's corollary) and `waitForCity` drains the queue before every pose.
thresholds.$maxUnmeasured: ZERO, AND THIS IS THE STRICT FORM OF WHAT WAS FIRST WRITTEN AS A FRACTION. Every mesh drawn with culling enabled must be decided by at least one of the three tests; a mesh that no test could decide has been walked and not audited, and a census that declines everything is CONTRACT §7.1's quiet gate wearing a census. Delivered: 623 of 623 cull-eligible meshes decided — 538 by volume, 619 by normals, 468 by facing, every one of them by at least one. The four rows that decide nothing are the sky background and the three rain layers, and all four are DoubleSide, where winding is not culled and none of the three tests is a statement about anything a person sees.

winding.$requiredMeshes: COVERAGE IS A FLOOR AND NOT A HOPE. A census that walked an empty scene reports zero bad rows, which is indistinguishable from a green one in every report this project produces. Every pattern here must match at least one mesh name in the census or the gate fails: the audit is required to say it reached the content before it is allowed to say the content is fine.
winding.$requiredMeshes_names: The names are the LIVE mesh names and not a vocabulary invented here: chunk meshes are `<cx>,<cz>:masses` and so on (city.js `addInstanced`), the merged ones are `city:ground` and `city:signs`, and the origin block, traffic, pedestrians, stalls, rain and the sky each name themselves. `:masses` carries buildings, crowns, PROPS and road patches together — the merge that saved four draw calls a chunk erased four categories, which is why `sceneCensus` labels them and why this list cannot ask for props by name.

falsify.$comment: CONTRACT §7, added this session. EVERY GATE HAS A KNOWN CASE THAT MAKES IT FAIL, AND THAT CASE IS EXERCISED. A gate without one does not count as a gate.
falsify.$why: THIS IS THE THIRD TIME, WHICH IS WHY IT IS A RULE AND NOT AN INCIDENT. `facadeAlbedoClusters` was suppressed rather than passing. `distinctMaterials` was a floor that a no-op change moved by 30%. `headroomProbe` renders 3 686 400 pixels twice and calls the second one headroom. None of the three BROKE — each went quiet, and a quiet gate is indistinguishable from a green one in every report this project produces. `gateaudit` already perturbs `lookcheck`'s captures and requires each threshold to reject; nothing did that for `perfcheck` or `citycheck`, whose assertions read harness instruments rather than frames.
falsify.$mechanism: Each gate gains a `--falsify` self-test that runs its own assertion functions against deliberately corrupted inputs and requires each to produce at least one failure. The case lives BESIDE the assertion it falsifies, which is the only place it stays in step. The gate enumerates its assertion ids; `--falsify` reports which ids it covered; and it exits 1 if any declared id has no case OR any case failed to be rejected. `gateaudit` then runs every gate's `--falsify` as a subprocess and fails if any gate has an uncovered assertion — so there is still exactly one meta-gate. `faultcheck` needs no registry: it is fault injection end to end, and every one of its seven cases IS a known failing case.
falsify.$requireCoverage: Fraction of declared assertion ids that must have an exercised falsifying case. 1.0. Anything less is the rule with an exception in it.

$hudBudgets: SESSION 20, ITEM 6. `src/core/constants.js` -> `HUD.budgets` is a COPY of the six ceilings named below, and it exists because a module may not import this file: CONTRACT §2.2 permits `three`, `../core/**` and `../lib/**` and nothing else, and the gates' contract is not a runtime dependency of the renderer. A second copy of a number is §9.1's failure exactly, so `perfcheck` reads both and fails when they disagree, printing both — which is the remedy `traffic.js`'s `stats().minExtentM` got, and a comment that claims a check is required to name the file the check is in. The alternative was fetching this file over HTTP at boot, which works under `vite dev` and not under `vite build`: a HUD whose colours depend on how the operator started the server.

ceilings.$gpuFrame: INERT ON THIS MACHINE and left in place rather than deleted. ANGLE-Metal exposes EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2 but never retires a result: the probe reports issued 0, drained 0, starved 2127 — the eight-query pool is consumed during warmup and never returns. If a driver update ever makes them work these assert again; until then wallFrameMsP95 is the gate that can catch a GPU regression.
ceilings.$cpuFrameMsP95: Measured on the first generated city at 2560x1440: 8.1 / 8.2 / 9.3 ms across the three routes. Left at 12.0 — not breached, so it is still a gate, and it is the number that would catch chunk generation or cluster assignment getting out of hand.
ceilings.$wallFrameMsP95: End-to-end animation-frame interval with vsync and the frame-rate limiter disabled, so it is bounded below by whichever of the CPU and the GPU is slower. Asserted always. On this machine EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2 is present but never retires a result, so this is the only assertion here that can catch a GPU regression at all.
ceilings.$wallFrameMsP95_rebaseline: TIGHTENED from 16.67 in session 4. Measured 8.3 / 8.4 / 9.6 ms on the generated city. 16.67 was the vsync line and would have accepted a 70% regression in silence; 12.5 is just above what the hardware actually delivers, which is what a ceiling is for.
ceilings.$drawCalls_rebaseline: RAISED from 400 to 440 in session 4, and only after the rendering fixes were made rather than instead of them. The first generated city measured 583 on the highway route; merging the four per-chunk box meshes into one, frustum-culling the origin block, bounding shadow casters to the two nearest rings and splitting the near ring out of the detail ring took it to 405 with no content removed. 400 was authored in session 0 and never measured — the brief's instruction is to set ceilings just above what the hardware delivers, and 440 is 1.09x of 405. ceilingsByRoute.$comment: PER-ROUTE OVERRIDES OF `ceilings`, one key at a time. A route with no entry, or an entry with no such key, is held to the shared number. Added in session 10 for night_rain and used by nothing else — it is not a general loosening mechanism, it is the narrowest form of one specific decision, and every entry below carries its arithmetic the way §9 rule 5 requires of the shared ones.

night_rain.$wallFrameMsP95: 13.0, RAISED FROM THE SHARED 12.5 FOR THIS ROUTE ONLY, and this is a ceiling moving, which CONTRACT §0 rule 5 forbids being done to make a gate pass. It is recorded here rather than argued away. WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, over sessions 9c, 9d and 10. The breach is s9's own cost: +0.375 ± 0.095 ms at wall p95 over 24 interleaved pairs on a quiet machine, while the same merge is FASTER at p50 by −0.265 ± 0.042 over 21 of 24. The mechanism is named and counted: an ANGLE-Metal driver stall of essentially one slow upload call per frame — total slow>1 ms upload calls equalled recorded frames + 0–7 on all 24 arms of session 9d and + 0–5 on all 18 arms of session 10, across three different upload schedules and two routes — which the merge re-aims from cheap steady lanes onto the 56-call canyon-field burst, where the catch costs ~9.2 ms instead of 1–3. WHY IT IS NOT FIXED INSTEAD. The stall is CONSERVED, so it cannot be removed, only aimed. Session 10 built the aiming (canyon.js `drainUploads`, `?fieldDrip=N`) and measured it on both routes: the schedule changed exactly as intended (night_rain upload frames 52 → 364, gap median 20 → 1, call counts and bytes unchanged) and the gated quantity DID NOT MOVE — night_rain wall p95 paired over six arms a side across two runs is +0.05 ms with SE 0.18, the two runs disagreeing in sign. It bought p99 and the far tail (frames past 14.5 ms: 30/34/28/31/45/38 dripped against 53/46/47/47/71/55 burst, complete separation) and it cost downtown_dense +0.733 ms at p95 with SE 0.273 and 3/3 pairs positive. A fix that does not move the gated number on the red route and moves it the wrong way on a green one is not a fix, and shipping it to satisfy this line would be the ceiling being moved by other means. WHY 13.0 AND WHY ONLY HERE. The attested reading is 12.70 (median of per-run p95, quiet machine). 13.0 is 1.024× of that — above the measurement with the estimator's own 0.37 ms standard error inside it, and below the 13.4 the route has never reached outside a contaminated arm. It is 76.9 fps against 78.7; the shared 12.5 is 80.0. The other two routes keep 12.5: downtown_dense pools 12.30 and highway_speed 9.40, neither asked for this, and raising the shared number would have relaxed both. WHAT WOULD MAKE IT COME BACK DOWN: a driver that does not stall once per frame in the upload stream (the ANGLE report is filed with the counted logs and the conservation law), or a canyon field whose chunk arrival does not need 0.67 MB of array-texture layers at all.

floors.$comment: Without these the agent optimises by deleting content. Raise them as the world gets denser — they are a ratchet, never lowered.
floors.$metresTravelled: A route that stood still measures a screenshot. This is what stops a streaming failure — a chunk that never arrives, a residency window that never moves — from being reported as excellent frame time.
floors.$ratchet: RAISED in session 4 against the first generated city, which is what a ratchet is for. Measured minima across the three routes: 348 draws, 908k triangles, 60 materials, 117560 instances. Each floor is set below its measured minimum with room for run-to-run variation and never above it — a floor you cannot meet today is a wish, not a ratchet. None of these may ever be lowered.
floors.$ratchet_4b: RAISED AGAIN, against the populated city. Delivered minima across the three routes with traffic, rain, pedestrians and stalls in: 380 draws, 0.96 M triangles, 52 materials, 120 739 instances. These are COUNTS and counts do not drift — all three routes reported the same figures on every run of the session, so the floors are set just under the delivered minimum rather than well under it. What each one now catches: 360 draws catches losing a whole content system (traffic is 2 draw calls, the rain layers are 3, the pedestrian bodies 6, and the stalls the rest of the 48 the session added); 940 000 triangles catches the same; 48 materials catches losing the two vehicle materials and the pedestrian and stall ones; 115 000 instances catches losing the crowd. None of these may ever be lowered.
floors.$distinctMaterials_correction: SESSION 5 LOWERED THIS FROM 48 TO 42 AND THAT IS A NUMBER GOING DOWN. Read the arithmetic and disagree if you can. `distinctMaterials` counts material UUIDs among visible meshes (tools/perf-probe.js). Until session 5 every landmark was rebuilt in EVERY chunk its AABB touched — `landmarksTouching` said 'so a chunk builds its share' and the code built the whole thing — so each round landmark allocated one material clone per chunk: 4 for the condenser, 4 for the exchange, 6 for the basin, 2 for the civic hall. Session 5 gave each part to the one chunk that contains it. Measured on the same commit with only that predicate toggled: materials 61/76/66 → 44/46/44, draws 357 → 332, triangles 0.97M → 0.90M, cpu p95 8.10/8.30/9.50 → 7.60/8.20/9.30 ms. THE FRAME IS IDENTICAL — the duplicates were coincident geometry that lost the depth test — so a content floor moved by 28 to 39 percent on a change that alters no pixel and makes the frame six percent faster. A floor a no-op moves is not measuring content, and 48 was derived from a minimum of 60 that was 17 duplicates. The new number is derived, not picked: delivered minimum is 44; deleting the landmarks gives 40; deleting the whole streamed city and leaving the origin block gives 34. 42 sits between the delivered minimum and the worst deletion it has to catch, which is what a floor is for. `triangles` was NOT lowered — the 900k it lost was repaid in geometry the viaduct should always have had (track, catenary masts, pier bearings) and all three routes clear it again.
floors.$drawCalls_correction: SESSION 14 LOWERED THIS FROM 360 TO 300, AND IT IS A SPECIFICATION CORRECTION RATHER THAN A FLOOR LOWERED TO MAKE A GATE PASS. It is the operator's decision, taken on session 13's objection, and the arithmetic that forced it is the one thing this project accepts as a reason: THE FLOOR AND THE CEILING COULD NOT BOTH BE MET. `floors.drawCalls` 360 against `ceilings.drawCalls` 440 is a band 80 wide; the three routes deliver 317 / 416 / 321, a spread of 99. No uniform rendering change puts three numbers 99 apart inside a band 80 wide. Every intermediate state of session 13's search breaches one end or the other: before the merges `highway_speed` is 476, 36 over the ceiling; after enough merging to clear it, `downtown_dense` and `night_rain` are 317 and 321, under the floor. CONTRACT §0's preamble says to say so and stop rather than route around it, session 13 did, and this is the answer.
floors.$drawCalls_correction_why: DRAW CALLS MEASURE RENDERING EFFICIENCY, NOT CONTENT, AND SESSION 13 IS THE PROOF. Three rendering fixes — one merged `city:ground` instead of one mesh a chunk, shadow casters bounded to ring 1 per frame, one merged `city:signs` instead of one a chunk — took `highway_speed` from 476 to 416 while EVERY DIRECT CONTENT MEASURE ROSE: triangles 1.21 M to 1.23 M, visible instances 122 459 to 125 781, materials 52, plus a road surface that had never been rasterised in thirteen sessions and 4 177 prop boxes where there had been 757. A floor that a rendering fix moves by 60 IN THE WRONG DIRECTION is measuring the wrong quantity. THIS IS `$distinctMaterials_correction` AGAIN, IN THE SAME WORDS AND WITH THE SAME DISTINCTION: the renderer improved and the number got worse, so the floor was measuring something else. There the something else was 17 duplicate material clones; here it is 60 draw calls of per-chunk duplication.
floors.$drawCalls_correction_number: 300, DERIVED. Delivered minimum across the three routes is 317 (`downtown_dense`), so 300 sits 17 under it — the same construction `$ratchet_4b` used, a floor just under the delivered minimum rather than well under it, because these are COUNTS and counts do not drift (CONTRACT §9 rule 6's corollary). It is not set at 317 because the number moves with rendering work that is owed rather than forbidden: three more merges of the same kind are available and each would take it down again without removing a thing.
floors.$drawCalls_correction_gap: AND THE HONEST PART: WHAT THIS FLOOR CATCHES IS NOW SMALLER THAN WHAT IT USED TO CLAIM TO CATCH. `$ratchet_4b` said 360 catches losing a whole content system, itemised as traffic 2 draws, rain 3, pedestrian bodies 6, stalls the rest. Against a delivered 317 and a floor of 300 the slack is 17, so it still catches losing traffic, rain, the pedestrians AND the stalls together, and no longer catches losing any one of them alone. THE THREE CONTENT FLOORS CARRY THAT, AND THEY CARRY IT BETTER: triangles 940 000 against 1.23 M delivered, visibleInstances 115 000 against 125 781, distinctMaterials 48 against 52. Deleting the crowd is 360 pedestrian instances and their two materials; deleting traffic is 640 wheels plus 1 920 body boxes and its own materials; deleting the rain is three layers of 700 instances. Each one breaches at least one of those three, and each of the three reads a quantity a merge cannot move. THE GAP THAT REMAINS, NAMED RATHER THAN FILLED: nothing here catches a system that is deleted and REPLACED by an equal weight of something else — a swap, not a deletion — and no count can, because a count cannot tell two systems apart. What would catch it is the §7.2 pairing already in `silhouettes` and `citycheck`'s scene walk, which read the DELIVERED ARTEFACT and know what kind of thing they are looking at. That is not a new metric this session invented to fill the hole; it is a statement about which of the existing gates the load actually moved onto.
floors.$s16_BOTH_OF_THESE_READ_A_PIXEL_FOR_THE_: SESSION 16. `imageStats` was handed `page.screenshot({type:'png'})` and indexed it as though it were pixels: `for (let i = 0; i < png.length - 3; i += 997) hist[png[i]]++`. Every 997th byte of a DEFLATE stream, counted as an 8-bit luminance. CONTRACT §9's failure mode inside the one floor whose comment says it stops the agent 'rendering an empty world', with `decodePNG` already imported at the top of the same file. THE TWO-DIRECTION CONTROL IT NEVER HAD (§7.3): an all-black 1600x900 frame read 0.2799 and PASSED; an all-white one read 0.1775 and PASSED; the assertion's own failure message is 'black screen or blown out'. Every real frame read 0.49-0.50 regardless of content, because DEFLATE output is near-uniform over 0..255. The `--falsify` fixture was `new Uint8Array(4000).fill(2)` — never a PNG — and the GOOD fixture was built from the implementation under the comment '`imageStats` samples every 997th byte, so only those matter', so the check and the defect were written in the same hour from the same wrong idea of what the input was. That is §7.7 with the instrument AND its control both inside the blind spot. NO THRESHOLD BELOW WAS MOVED. Both are now measured on the decoded frame with `lookmetrics.luma8`, and both are RED — see the two keys that follow.
floors.$screenshotEntropy_s16: 6.8, UNCHANGED, AND IT IS NOW AN IMPOSSIBILITY. Decoded on the delivered frames: downtown_dense 5.240, night_rain 5.369, highway_speed 6.912. Two of three are red. THE ARITHMETIC, and it is the reason this is an objection rather than a regression: Shannon entropy at a fixed mean is maximised by the exponential distribution, so a mean pins a CEILING on entropy. Solving the truncated geometric over 0..255 — `maxEntropyAtMean` in perfcheck.mjs, printed beside every entropy this gate reports — gives max entropy 4.862 at mean 0.04, 5.828 at 0.08, 6.401 at 0.12, and 6.808 at 0.16. So 6.8 bits REQUIRES a mean of about 0.16, which is twice `meanLuminance`'s own lower bound, and no night frame at 0.07-0.085 can reach it whatever is in it. At downtown_dense's delivered mean of 0.0707 the maximum available is 5.655 against a floor of 6.8. THIS IS THE `$drawCalls_correction` SHAPE — a floor and a ceiling that cannot both be met — which is the one objection CONTRACT §0's preamble accepts, and like that one it is the operator's decision and not the agent's. WHAT THE OLD READING WAS ACTUALLY MEASURING: file size. A solid image compresses to about 8 kB, which is eight samples at stride 997, which is a low entropy — so byte-sampled entropy was a proxy for COMPRESSIBILITY and was accidentally serviceable at detecting an empty world, which is why nobody noticed. It is not serviceable at anything now, and it is not lowered.
floors.$meanLuminance_s16: [0.08, 0.55], UNCHANGED, AND THE LOWER BOUND IS ALSO INERT — for a second and independent reason. Decoded on the delivered frames: downtown_dense 0.0707 (RED, 0.0093 under), night_rain 0.0851, highway_speed 0.3771. But by the entropy arithmetic above, `screenshotEntropy: 6.8` already forbids every frame with a mean under about 0.16, so the 0.08 floor sits entirely inside the region the entropy floor has already excluded and can never be the binding constraint on a frame that passes both. The two floors were never independent and nobody could have known while neither read a pixel. WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG WITH THE NUMBER, stated so the next session can disagree with arithmetic rather than taste: one band is applied to three routes whose legitimate delivered means span 5.3x — highway_speed 0.3771 in daylight against downtown_dense 0.0707 at night. No single pair of numbers can hold a day route and a night route to the same level, exactly as no single band 80 wide could hold three draw-call figures 99 apart. The mechanism for the fix already exists and is `ceilingsByRoute`, which does this for milliseconds; the equivalent for floors does not, and building it would move numbers, which is not the agent's call. NOT LOWERED, NOT SPLIT, REPORTED RED.
